item.excerpt:encoded: J. Donald Monan, S.J., assumed the newly created post of Chancellor in August, 1996, following 24 years as Boston College President—the longest presidential tenure in the University’s history. Prior to joining Boston College in August, 1972, Father Monan held positions as Acting President, Vice President, Academic Dean, Chairman of the Philosophy Department, Professor and Instructor at Le Moyne College in New York, and Instructor of Philosophy at St. Peter’s College in New Jersey. Father Monan entered the Society of Jesus in 1942 and was ordained to the priesthood in 1955. He holds A.B., Ph.L. and S.T.L. degrees from Woodstock College and a Ph.D. degree from the University of Louvain in Belgium. In addition, he has conducted postdoctoral research at numerous universities. He is former chairman of the National Association of Independent Colleges and Universities and of the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, served as a director of the Bank of Boston (1976-96), as interim president of the Association of Jesuit Colleges and Universities (1996-97), and co-chair of the Massachusetts Summit for the Promise of our Youth (1997). He currently serves on the Board of Directors of One to One/The National Mentoring Partnership, of the Massachusetts Mentoring Partnership, of which he served as co-chair from 1992-2001, of the Naval Academy Endowment Trust, of the Yawkey Foundation, and on the Board of Trustees and Executive Committee of Le Moyne College. Father Monan is also a member of the Jesuit Philosophical Association, the Society of Phenomenology and Existential Philosophy, the Society of Ancient Greek Philosophy, and the Massachusetts Historical Society. Photographed for Boston College Magazine, Fall 2012 issue.

Adopt a critical perspective

Adopt a critical perspective and add a different point of view to the discussion with a relentless focus on what’s ethical and in the best interest of students.

We have been quite critical... and that critical aspect I think has always been a very important basis for the center... and because I am responsible to nobody for nothing, we can just say what we want. And, we've been very happy to do that over time.

Phil Tweet

We always look into what, from our perspective, is ethically the right approach to take.

Hans Tweet

Don’t be afraid to challenge the mainstream. Be bold and fearless. Maintain intellectual independence. Advocate for what you believe is in the best interest of students. Stake out a position and be clear where you stand, even if you are in the minority. Embrace critical perspectives and consider the benefits and potential risks of different practices. How can you apply a critical perspective in your own work or educational setting to promote ethical practices?

item.title: Adopt a critical perspective
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
Adopt a critical perspective

Adopt a critical perspective and add a different point of view to the discussion with a relentless focus on what’s ethical and in the best interest of students.

We have been quite critical... and that critical aspect I think has always been a very important basis for the center... and because I am responsible to nobody for nothing, we can just say what we want. And, we've been very happy to do that over time.

Phil Tweet

We always look into what, from our perspective, is ethically the right approach to take.

Hans Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Appreciate the complexity of context

“We want to understand the complexity of context and what does that mean in the relationships, that we have as institutions of higher education, as systems of higher education, and how we have to relate that to policy making in the real world.” – Hans

item.title: History of the Center for International Higher Education
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
History of the Center for International Higher Education

1994-1999: Start of CIHE

1994

Philip G. Altbach joins Boston College faculty in 1994 from the State University of New York at Buffalo.

 

1994

1995

Altbach Appointed J. Donald Monan, SJ University Professor

Philip Altbach appointed the first J. Donald Monan, SJ University Professor in 1995. The Monan Chair provided a graduate assistant position, half-time administrative assistant, and funds to be used at the discretion of the Chair.

1995

CIHE Established

The Center for International Higher Education (CIHE) is established in 1995, with Philip Altbach as director. The Center is allocated office space at 207 Campion Hall. The Center’s staff included Philip Altbach as director, Salina Kopellas as administrative assistant, and two graduate assistants, one funded by the Monan Chair and one by the School of Education.

First Issue of International Higher Education

In 1995, the first issue of ‘International Higher Education’ is published by CIHE through the BC Library System.

1996

Ford Foundation

In approximately 1996, a grant from the Ford Foundation is obtained for basic CIHE support. This grant continued for about 15 years with several renewals and a total allocation of about $1 million. The grant provided an additional GA position and funds for research and general support for CIHE.

1996

In 1996, CIHE hosts its first professional development program, a program for senior administrators of the University of Amsterdam that aimed at providing an introduction to American higher education management.

Garland Studies in Higher Education

Throughout the 1990s, CIHE published its own books and distributes them without cost to readers and libraries in emerging economies, thanks to funding from the Ford Foundation grant. CIHE also sponsors another book series, Garland Studies in Higher Education, during this period.

1998

The first of many research-based conferences was held at BC in June 1998 on the topic of private higher education. The methodology used for this conference was later used for other CIHE projects—asking researchers to draft papers on a theme and discussing them at the conference and then revising for publication.

This conference included 50 researchers, policymakers, and leaders in private higher education from around the world. Main funding came from the Ford Foundation. Private Prometheus: Private Higher Education and Development in the 21st Century (Greenwood, 1999) included the papers from the conference.

1998

2000-2015: Expansion and Enhancement

2000

CIHE has been concerned with developing the field of international higher education since its establishment and over the years has put together several inventories of centers and programs in the field, all funded internally.  The first is published in 2000.

2000

2004

New Century Scholars

In 2004, Philip Altbach is selected by the Fulbright agency to be the Distinguished Scholar Leader of the Fulbright New Century Scholars program, a two-year program that selected 31 scholars from around the world to work together on higher education themes. Three conferences, one at BC, were organized, along with various research themes.

2004

2005

Global Perspectives on Higher Education

In 2005, a new book series, initially published by Sense Publishers, Global Perspectives on Higher Education, is launched.

2005

2007

In 2007, Laura Rumbley is hired as research associate of CIHE, after BC approves an additional staff member.

2007

2008

Beginning in 2008, a 28-country comparative study of academic salaries is cosponsored (and mainly funded) by the Higher School of Economics in Moscow, with a working conference held in Moscow. This marks the first of many joint CIHE-HSE projects.

 

In 2008, CIHE signs an agreement with Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China to produce a Chinese translation of IHE, the first of many translations produced by partners around the world.

2008

2012

Laura Rumbley returns in 2012 as Associate Director, a position she held until 2018.

2012

2013

Philip G. Altbach Retires

In 2013, Philip G. Altbach retires from his tenured full-time professorship as the Monan Chair and is appointed Research Professor at BC. From 2013 to 2015, he continues as director of CIHE

2013

In 2013, IHE is launched electronically, via the BC library system.

 

2014

Beginning in 2014, the Carnegie Corporation of New York, through its Africa program, provides funding to CIHE for work focused specifically on Africa. This project, coordinated by former CIHE doctoral graduate Damtew Teferra, from his position at Kwazulu Natal University, produced three HEFAALA (Higher Education Forum for Africa, Asia and Latin America) conferences and supported the launch of the International Journal of African Higher Education and the International Network for African Higher Education.

2014

2015-2020: New Leadership and Further Expansion and Innovation

2015

Hans de Wit Appointed

In 2015, Hans de Wit is appointed CIHE Director and Professor of the Practice in the Lynch School of Education.

2015

2016

Dual Degree Program

In 2016, new academic programs in International Higher Education are launched, including a Certificate program, an MA program (now a specialist track through the MA in Higher Education) and a Dual Degree program with the Universidad de Guadalajara in Mexico.

2016

CIHE Perspectives

In 2016, CIHE launches an in-house open access series, CIHE Perspectives, which publishes work by CIHE staff and affiliates, as well as the proceedings of conferences sponsored by the Center.

WES-CIHE Summer Institute

In 2016, CIHE, in cooperation with and sponsored by World Education Services (WES) launches the annual WES-CIHE Summer Institute for early career researchers. The Summer Institute represents one of CIHE’s key missions, i.e. to support the next generation of international higher education researchers around the world.

2017

In 2017, the Center launches a new book series, Studies in International Higher Education, in collaboration with the Centre for Global Higher Education at the Institute of Education, London. The series ends in 2023 when Sage India stops publishing books, although all books in the initial series are now available open access on the CIHE website.

2017

2018

Betty Leask Visiting Professor

From 2018 to 2020, CIHE benefits from the presence of Betty Leask, Emerita Professor in International Higher Education at La Trobe University in Melbourne, Australia, who assumes the role of Visiting Professor.

2018

2019

Rebecca Schendel Appointed

In 2019, Laura Rumbley leaves BC, and Rebecca Schendel is appointed as her successor.

2019

2020s: A New Leadership Model

2020

In Spring 2020, after being published independently by CIHE for 25 years, IHE begins to be published by DUZ Academic Publishers in Berlin, Germany, however with editorial independence fully intact. In the same year, and as the first issue under the new publisher, IHE’s 100 issue is published: ‘Unprecedented Challenges, Significant Opportunities?’

2020

Gerardo Blanco Appointed

In November 2020, Hans de Wit steps down as CIHE Director of CIHE. The Center is reorganized with a distributed leadership structure. Gerardo Blanco – newly appointed Associate Professor of Higher Education – and Rebecca Schendel – former Associate Director – assume the roles of Academic and Managing Directors, respectively.

2021

In 2021, CIHE assembles an Advisory Board to support the Center leadership in the development of long-term strategy and the identification of important global trends.

2021

In 2021, the Educational Leadership and Higher Education Department in the Lynch School starts a new Executive EdD program in Higher Education. Chris R. Glass is hired as Director of the EdD program.

In response to the challenges of connecting internationally during the COVID-19 pandemic, the Center launches a monthly webinar series. The model’s success ensures that it continues, even after the public health situation improves.

2022

Hans de Wit Fellowship

In 2022, CIHE launches the Hans de Wit Fellowship for Visiting Scholars, funded by World Education Services, a fellowship which intends to support early career scholars in higher education studies with 4 months of scholarship at CIHE. The first fellow, Sevgi Kaya-Kasikci, arrives in March 2023.

2022

2023

Biennial CIHE Conference

The inaugural Biennial CIHE Conference on International Higher Education is held. The event brings together higher education researchers from around the world, in order to foster new connections and spark new research collaborations.

2023

Philip G. Altbach Lecture

During the inaugural conference, the Philip G. Altbach Lecture is launched, an annual lecture that honors Phil’s leading and founding role in the field of international higher education. Simon Marginson of the University of Oxford is selected as the first speaker in the Altbach Lecture series.

\u00a0<\/p>","_id":"4c7eef1"},{"timeline_single_date":"1995","timeline_single_heading":"Altbach Appointed J. Donald Monan, SJ University Professor","timeline_single_content":"Philip Altbach appointed the first J. Donald Monan, SJ University Professor in 1995. The Monan Chair provided a graduate assistant position, half-time administrative assistant, and funds to be used at the discretion of the Chair.<\/span>

<\/p>","_id":"86c49c8"},{"timeline_single_heading":"CIHE Established","timeline_single_content":"

<\/p>

The Center for International Higher Education (CIHE) is established in 1995, with Philip Altbach as director. The Center is allocated office space at 207 Campion Hall. The Center\u2019s staff included Philip Altbach as director, Salina Kopellas as administrative assistant, and two graduate assistants, one funded by the Monan Chair and one by the School of Education.<\/p>","_id":"8bf56d4"},{"_id":"7899c36","timeline_single_heading":"First Issue of International Higher Education","timeline_single_content":"

<\/p>

In 1995, the first issue of \u2018International Higher Education\u2019 is published by CIHE through the BC Library System.<\/p>"},{"_id":"898062f","timeline_single_date":"1996","timeline_single_heading":"Ford Foundation","timeline_single_content":"

<\/p>

In approximately 1996, a grant from the Ford Foundation is obtained for basic CIHE support. This grant continued for about 15 years with several renewals and a total allocation of about $1 million. The grant provided an additional GA position and funds for research and general support for CIHE.<\/p>"},{"_id":"19aaeb0","timeline_single_content":"

<\/p>

In 1996, CIHE hosts its first professional development program, a program for senior administrators of the University of Amsterdam that aimed at providing an introduction to American higher education management.<\/p>"},{"_id":"0cd10e0","timeline_single_heading":"Garland Studies in Higher Education","timeline_single_content":"

Throughout the 1990s, CIHE published its own books and distributes them without cost to readers and libraries in emerging economies, thanks to funding from the Ford Foundation grant. CIHE also sponsors another book series, Garland Studies in Higher Education<\/em>, during this period.<\/p>"},{"_id":"feaf5a4","timeline_single_date":"1998","timeline_single_content":"

<\/p>

The first of many research-based conferences was held at BC in June 1998 on the topic of private higher education. The methodology used for this conference was later used for other CIHE projects\u2014asking researchers to draft papers on a theme and discussing them at the conference and then revising for publication.<\/p>

This conference included 50 researchers, policymakers, and leaders in private higher education from around the world. Main funding came from the Ford Foundation. Private Prometheus: Private Higher Education and Development in the 21st Century<\/i><\/span> (Greenwood, 1999) included the papers from the conference.<\/p>"}],"no_results_text":"Sorry, we couldn't find any posts. <\/p>

In 2004, Philip Altbach is selected by the Fulbright agency to be the Distinguished Scholar Leader of the Fulbright New Century Scholars program, a two-year program that selected 31 scholars from around the world to work together on higher education themes. In 2007, Laura Rumbley is hired as research associate of CIHE, after BC approves an additional staff member.<\/p>"},{"_id":"737cc87","timeline_single_date":"2008","timeline_single_content":"

Beginning in 2008, a 28-country comparative study of academic salaries is cosponsored (and mainly funded) by the Higher School of Economics in Moscow, with a working conference held in Moscow. This marks the first of many joint CIHE-HSE projects.<\/p>

\u00a0<\/p>

In 2008, CIHE signs an agreement with Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China to produce a Chinese translation of IHE<\/em>, the first of many translations produced by partners around the world.<\/p>"},{"_id":"6cda866","timeline_single_date":"2012","timeline_single_content":"

History of International Higher Education

1950s

Massive expansion of higher education institutions globally

Trends:

  • Establishment of international organizations and student exchange programs
  • Growing emphasis on research and knowledge creation
  • Increasing demand for lifelong learning and continuing education

 

Tensions

  • Standardization vs. localization in emerging education systems
  • Influence of political ideology on higher education vs. academic autonomy and independence

1960s

The emergence of comparative education as a distinct discipline

Trends:

  • Post-colonial nation-building and the role of education in newly independent states
  • International development and the influence of education on economic growth
  • Cultural exchanges and international cooperation in education

 

Tensions

  • Balancing national identity and global influences in newly independent states
  • Standardization vs. localization in emerging education systems

1970s

Equity and access to higher education across gender, race, and socioeconomic status

Trends:

  • Influence of international organizations on education policies
    Impact of global economic crisis on higher education systems
    Role of education in the promotion of human rights and social justice

 

Tensions:

  • Global economic crisis: investment in education vs. austerity measures
  • Equity and access vs. limited resources in higher education

1980s

Marketization and privatization of higher education

Trends:

  • Integration of technology and innovations in higher education
  • The role of higher education in addressing global environmental challenges
  • Comparative assessment of quality and effectiveness of different education systems

 

Tensions:

  • Marketization and privatization vs. public responsibility in higher education
  • Environmental challenges vs. economic development in education policies

1990s

Globalization and its impact on higher education

Trends:

  • Internationalization of curricula and the emergence of cross-border education
  • The role of higher education in fostering global citizenship
  • Shift from input-oriented to outcome-oriented approaches in higher education

 

Tensions:

  • Globalization and its impact on local cultures and traditions in higher education
  • Internationalization vs. national priorities in curricula

2000s

The rise of massification and expansion of higher education

Trends:

  • The knowledge economy and the role of higher education in promoting innovation
  • Accountability, quality assurance, and accreditation in higher education
  • Impact of international rankings on higher education policies and practices

 

Tensions:

  • Massification and expansion of higher education vs. quality and accessibility
  • International rankings vs. diverse education systems and goals

2010s

Digitalization and the rise of online and blended learning models

Trends:

  • International student mobility and brain circulation
  • New forms of international partnerships and collaborations in higher education
  • Addressing the skills gap and the relevance of higher education to the labor market

 

Tensions:

  • Global collaboration vs. competition in higher education
  • Digitalization and online learning vs. traditional classroom experiences

2020s

The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on higher education

Trends:

  • Equity and inclusion in the digital era of higher education
  • Sustainability and the role of higher education in addressing global challenges
  • The future of international higher education in a rapidly changing world

 

Tensions:

  • COVID-19 pandemic: adaptation and resilience vs. maintaining quality in higher education
  • Sustainability and global challenges vs. economic pressures in higher education

item.title: Harness the power of social movements
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
Harness the power of social movements

Recognize the power of activism in driving social, political, and educational transformations, and use it as a tool to create meaningful impact. Activism is more than protest. It is network and coalition building. Be a force for change; build lasting coalitions.

I learned much of what I know, what I've done over the years through, the social movements that I was involved in. I've always had a kind of a political social interest in my scholarship and work.

Phil Tweet

My dissertation was on student political activism, stemming from my own involvement in student political activism in the United States when I was a student, and at the time I got into it, there was really nobody doing serious research and analysis of that topic, especially in an international perspective.

Phil Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Know the power of symbol

“I noticed that the symbol that they were using, which was ubiquitous all over the place, the flags and all kinds of things was this, what’s now called the peace symbol in this country.” – Phil

Advocate without owning

Advocating for critical issues without claiming ownership fosters a more inclusive and dynamic field.

How do we advocate, how do we push for something without owning it? I never would want to be the person that owns or gatekeeps knowledge on a particular area... Because once you own it, you limit new possibilities.

Gerardo Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Foster inclusive growth

“One of the ways that the field has grown has been actually the creation of higher education centers, that study higher education domestically, but in places where they haven’t done it before.” – Rebecca

Build networks

The Altbach method: gather people in a room to exchange ideas, build relationships, and harness the power of cross-border networks. Share knowledge, resources, and expertise. Gathered minds, multiply success.

I've always been interested in network building. I've always been interested in developing countries. I was always interested in research topics … that I thought had policy relevance and also were new, unresearched.

The center has always had this tradition of learning about higher education systems with people who work within those higher education systems.

item.title: Mentor the next generation of scholars​
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
Mentor the next generation of scholars

There has never been a master plan. Ask questions. Foster an environment where everyone contributes to the work. Engage graduate students as colleagues. Mentor the next generation of scholars and leaders.

There's never been a master plan… the grad students have ideas about what we should be doing and we either do them or not, depending on if it's practical.

Phil Tweet

You have an idea. Great! Let's do a project or a book out of it. You worked on this with me. Your name is going on this book.

Laura Tweet

I find it most rewarding when I have been able to help them with their PhD or their master thesis and have been successful… I have a strong international network of people who I consider much more as friends than us colleagues. That's so rewarding.

Hans Tweet

That was the case when Phil was the director. That was the case when Hans was the director. It's the case now, and I think it will always be the case because the next generation is involved.

Rebecca Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Smallness as a strength

“They were really surprised, always when they saw that this was our office… but we always then said, it might look like a weakness, but it is a strength.” – Hans

item.title: See smallness as a strength
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
See smallness as a strength

A small research center can have an outsized impact when it is resourceful. Smallness in size, when complemented with a broad network and collaboration, yields significant impact .

People used to come to the center and look around our offices, which are even as we speak today, very small, but wondering where our staff was, and I would tell them, ‘You're looking at it.’

Phil Tweet

He could take the tiniest budget and turn it into something incredibly long-lasting or incredibly multi-dimensional in its outputs on the basis of his own hard work, his enthusiasm, and his lack of need for a lot of money.

Laura Tweet

They were really surprised, always when they saw that this was our office... but we always then said, it might look like a weakness, but it is a strength.

Hans Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Build a culture of curiosity

“I have a lot of ideas, and, many of them, I push, and the only small percentage of that is happening, but it is much better to do that than having just one or two ideas in your life and, even if you’re not always successful or too limited in your approach.” – Hans

The growth and development of the field is enhanced by the creation of domestic educational centers in regions previously underrepresented. By focusing on domestic contexts and encouraging unique perspectives, we enrich the collective understanding of global higher education.

One of the ways that the field has grown has been actually the creation of higher education centers, that study higher education domestically, but in places where they haven't done it before.

item.content:encoded:
Evolve leadership to meet new realities

The center is not a person but a set of values reimagined in three generations of leadership. Succession is passing those values to the next generation.

We're now into our third leadership team. When Hans left, there was no debate about whether the center should continue, and that's, I think, a significant accomplishment.

Phil Tweet

He kept saying all the time over the five years, go and do what you want to do.

Hans Tweet

We have shifted from a one director structure to a distributed leadership structure. We say this all the time, the center is the network… the network is going to continue no matter what.

Rebecca Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Engage with the Global South

“From the start, it has been always very much engaged with the Global South, and that has always been part of my approach in internationalization.” – Hans

Recognize the unsustainability of the market-driven approach to internationalization. Use analysis as a tool to guide and shape practical solutions to shift towards ethical and inclusive internationalization.

Internationalization over the past decades has moved from a much more cooperative exercise of, exchange of students, exchange of faculty joint curriculum development to a competitive marketization.

item.title: Embrace diverse perspectives
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
Embrace diverse perspectives

The growth of the field of international higher education necessitates the inclusion and understanding of diverse perspectives. While the task is challenging and wide-ranging, it is crucial for the development of a more comprehensive and inclusive understanding of the field.

As the field grows, there are more and more different perspectives that are represented. But that in itself is a lot of work, let alone knowing and understanding faculty issues and understanding students, nobody can really do all of that.

Gerardo Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Nothing beyond Beethoven

“My view generally speaking is that any composer post Ludvig van Beethoven is not interesting, and I would not listen to it voluntarily.” – Phil

item.content:encoded:
Take a chance on technology

New technologies open new forms of communication, collaboration, and dissemination of knowledge.

In the early days of the internet, I mean the very early days, one of my doc students came to me and said, ‘Hey, Phil, we should put this on the internet and have a website.' And this was when websites were not common. And I said, if it doesn't take too much time, go ahead, have fun . And it turned out to be one of the most important things we did, of course.

Phil Tweet

Now it's impossible to think of the work that we do. Without leveraging these new emerging technologies that are not so emerging.

Gerardo Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Advocate for open access to knowledge​

“We were committed from the first that it should be free, that access to international higher education should not cost anything to anybody.” – Phil

item.title: Advocate for open access to knowledge​
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
Advocate for open access to knowledge

Open access is essential to engage and share knowledge from — and relevant to — underrepresented regions and broaden our understanding of international higher education.

We were committed from the first that it should be free – that access to International Higher Education should not cost anything to anybody.

Phil Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Get real

“I also think there are other stakeholders for higher education that we’re not even considering yet. Think that’s going to be kind of a next level set of considerations to have for the future.” – Gerardo

item.title: Get real
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
Get real

Get real. Find a balance between conducting methodologically sound research and ensuring its relevance to non-academic audiences in the world of higher education and beyond.

I also think there are other stakeholders for higher education that we're not even considering yet. Think that's going to be kind of a next level set of considerations to have for the future.

Gerardo Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Speak to a broader audience

“I’ve always thought that was very important to engage with a broader higher ed audience and if possible, even in broader general audience around something which I think I knew about, which is higher education.” – Phil

Look down-the-road for important issues that are not on-the-radar but could have a major impact. Raise awareness about those issues. Don’t shy away from debate when important principles are at stake. Be critical but offer a vision of hope.

We've done that on a range of things, stimulated by life, you know, by what's happening in the world of higher education that we think needs focusing on, and to bring a, bring a kind of a different perspective.

Phil Tweet

I think right now I would just offer a vision of hope because I think it's easy not to have it right now.

Gerardo Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Build networks

“The center has always had this tradition of learning about higher education systems with people who work within those higher education systems.” -Rebecca

item.title: Speak to a broader audience
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
Speak to a broader audience

Communicate insights and knowledge beyond academia. Learn to write in a way that speaks to policymakers, government officials, and the public with actionable insights to influence decision-making on issues that matter.

I've always thought that was very important to engage with a broader higher ed audience and if possible, even in broader general audience around something which I think I knew about, which is higher education.

Phil Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Advocate without owning

“How do we advocate, how do we push for something without owning it? I never would want to be the person that owns or gatekeeps knowledge on a particular area… Because once you own it, you limit new possibilities.” – Gerardo

item.title: Build a culture of curiosity
item.dc:creator: glassch
item.content:encoded:
Build a culture of curiosity

Ask questions. Maintain a child-like curiosity. Build a culture that values continuous experimentation. Expand your knowledge of the world. Never stop exploring. ​

And he is one of the most prominent people I know that will genuinely ask you, "What are you doing?" "What do you think?" and "What would you do in my situation?"

Laura Tweet

I have a lot of ideas, and, many of them, I push, and the only small percentage of that is happening, but it is much better to do that than having just one or two ideas in your life and, even if you're not always successful or too limited in your approach.

Hans Tweet

Continue the Conversation

Take a chance on technology

In the early days of the internet, I mean the very early days, one of my doc students came to me and said, ‘Hey, Phil, we should put this on the internet and have a website.’ – Phil
